title: Deciduous & permanent dentitions
blurb: The 20 baby teeth, the 32 adult teeth, the mixed dentition in between, and why deciduous teeth matter.
question: A parent brings in their 6-year-old and points to a large new back tooth behind the baby teeth. 'It's only a baby tooth, so it doesn't matter if it gets a hole, does it?' What tooth is it most likely to be, and what should the parent understand?

teach.body: We grow two sets of teeth. The deciduous dentition (also called primary or milk teeth) has 20 teeth and is complete by about 2½ years. The permanent dentition has 32 teeth and replaces and adds to the first set from about 6 years. Between roughly 6 and 12 years a child has a mixed dentition: some deciduous teeth and some permanent teeth in the mouth at once. Knowing which set you are looking at matters for charting, for treatment and for advice to parents.

teach.caption: Five per quadrant, from the midline: central incisor, lateral incisor, canine, first molar, second molar. No premolars and no third molars.
Eight per quadrant. The highlighted premolars are new to this set: they erupt in place of the deciduous molars.

teach.body: Deciduous enamel and dentine are thin and the pulp is large, with pulp horns close to the surface. So decay in a baby tooth reaches the pulp quickly, and a small-looking cavity can soon cause pain or an abscess. Deciduous molar roots are short and flared outwards to leave room for the developing premolar underneath. As the permanent successor grows, it causes the deciduous root to resorb, and the loosened tooth is shed (exfoliated).

teach.note: Successional teeth (20) replace a deciduous tooth. The 12 permanent molars have no predecessor: they erupt behind the deciduous teeth as the jaws grow, so nothing is lost when they arrive.

teach.body: The first permanent molar erupts at about 6 years, behind the deciduous second molar, and no baby tooth is lost to make room for it. Parents often assume it is a baby tooth. It is permanent, it must last a lifetime, and its deep fissures are very prone to decay, so it is a priority for fissure sealing and fluoride. Pointing this out is a simple, valuable piece of oral health advice.

teach.text: Deciduous teeth are not 'just baby teeth'. They are needed for eating, speech and appearance, and they hold the space for the permanent teeth. Lose one early and neighbouring teeth can drift into the gap, leaving too little room for the successor and causing crowding.

items: Deciduous (primary) dentition: 20 teeth, complete by about 2½ years; no premolars.
Permanent dentition: 32 teeth; premolars replace deciduous molars.
Deciduous teeth: whiter, thinner enamel, larger pulps, short flared roots that resorb.
The first permanent molar erupts at about 6 behind the baby teeth: it is permanent.

summary: You can now give the number and types of teeth in each dentition, describe how deciduous teeth differ from permanent ones and why that matters for decay, explain successional and non-successional teeth, and correct the common belief that the six-year molar is a baby tooth.

A.q: How many teeth are there in a complete deciduous dentition?
A.why: There are five deciduous teeth in each quadrant, so 5 x 4 = 20.

whyNot.0: Sixteen would mean only four teeth per quadrant.
whyNot.1: Twenty-four would mean six per quadrant; deciduous quadrants have five.
whyNot.3: Twenty-eight is a permanent dentition without third molars.

A.q: Which tooth type is present in the permanent dentition but absent from the deciduous dentition?
A.why: There are no deciduous premolars. Permanent premolars erupt in place of the deciduous molars.

whyNot.0: There is one deciduous canine in each quadrant.
whyNot.2: Each deciduous quadrant has a lateral incisor.
whyNot.3: Each deciduous quadrant has a second molar.

A.q: Why can decay progress to the pulp more quickly in a deciduous molar than in a permanent molar?
options: Its enamel is thicker and more brittle
Its roots are longer and narrower
It has no dentinal tubules at all
Its enamel is thin and its pulp is large
A.why: Thin enamel and dentine over a relatively large pulp with high pulp horns mean decay reaches the pulp sooner.

whyNot.0: Deciduous enamel is thinner than permanent enamel, not thicker.
whyNot.1: Deciduous roots are shorter, and root length doesn't affect how fast crown decay spreads.
whyNot.2: Deciduous dentine has tubules, just like permanent dentine.

B.q: Which permanent teeth are NOT successional?
B.why: Permanent molars have no deciduous predecessor; they erupt behind the deciduous teeth as the jaw grows.

whyNot.1: Premolars replace the deciduous molars, so they are successional.

B.q: Roughly what age range describes the mixed dentition?
B.why: The mixed dentition runs from the first permanent teeth at about 6 until the last deciduous teeth are shed at about 12.

whyNot.0: This is when the deciduous teeth are erupting.
whyNot.1: In this period a child normally has only deciduous teeth.
whyNot.3: By this age the deciduous teeth have normally all been shed.

B.q: A deciduous molar is lost early to decay. What is the main concern for the permanent dentition?
options: The successor will erupt as a molar
Teeth drift and close the space
B.why: Deciduous teeth hold the space for their successors. If one is lost early, neighbours can drift into the gap and cause crowding.

whyNot.0: The successor of a deciduous molar is a premolar, whatever happens to the baby tooth.
whyNot.2: Early loss of the deciduous tooth doesn't stop the premolar developing.
whyNot.3: The gum heals over the socket, but the successor still erupts through it later.

C.q: Which teeth does a permanent premolar replace?
C.why: The permanent first and second premolars erupt in place of the deciduous first and second molars.

whyNot.0: Deciduous canines are replaced by permanent canines.
whyNot.1: Deciduous incisors are replaced by permanent incisors.
whyNot.2: Permanent teeth aren't replaced by other permanent teeth.

C.q: Which statement about deciduous teeth is correct?
options: Their roots are longer than permanent roots
They are whiter than permanent teeth
They have thicker enamel than adult teeth
They include two premolars per quadrant
C.why: Deciduous teeth look whiter and more milky than permanent teeth.

whyNot.0: Deciduous roots are shorter and thinner.
whyNot.2: Deciduous enamel is thinner than permanent enamel.

C.q: What causes a deciduous tooth to become loose before it is shed?
C.why: The developing permanent successor causes the deciduous root to resorb, so the tooth loosens and is exfoliated.

whyNot.1: Wear affects the crown and doesn't loosen the tooth.
whyNot.2: Pulp calcification is not the shedding mechanism.
whyNot.3: Gum recession is not how deciduous teeth are shed.

reteach.title: A starter kit and a full kit
reteach.question: Think of the deciduous teeth as a starter kit that keeps the places warm until the full adult kit arrives. What is in each kit?

blocks.body: A small jaw only has room for a small set: two incisors, a canine and two molars in each quarter, 20 in all. As the jaw grows, each starter tooth is swapped for an adult version, except that the two baby molars are swapped for premolars. Then three brand-new molars are added at the back of each quarter, where the jaw has grown, with nothing swapped out. 20 swaps plus 12 new molars gives the 32 adult teeth.

explain.body: Twenty teeth, five per quadrant: central incisor, lateral incisor, canine, first molar, second molar. Complete by about 2½ years. No premolars.

test.q: How many molars are in each quadrant of the deciduous dentition?
test.why: Each deciduous quadrant has a first and a second molar.

whyNot.0: There are two deciduous molars per quadrant, not one.
whyNot.1: Three molars per quadrant is the permanent pattern.
whyNot.3: Deciduous teeth include molars; they lack premolars.

explain.body: Whiter, smaller crowns with thinner enamel and dentine and a relatively large pulp. Roots are short and thin, and molar roots flare to make room for the premolar developing beneath. Decay reaches the pulp quickly.

explain.caption: With thin enamel and a large pulp, decay in a baby tooth reaches the pulp quickly.

test.q: Why are deciduous molar roots flared outwards?
options: To make room for the successor
test.why: The flared roots leave room between them for the developing premolar.

whyNot.1: The flare isn't there to improve grip in the socket.
whyNot.2: Root shape isn't about carrying extra vessels.
whyNot.3: The flare doesn't exist to house extra pulp.

explain.body: The 20 permanent incisors, canines and premolars replace deciduous teeth (successional). The 12 permanent molars have no predecessor and erupt behind the deciduous teeth (non-successional).

test.q: How many permanent teeth are successional?
test.why: All permanent teeth except the 12 molars replace a deciduous tooth: 32 minus 12 = 20.

whyNot.0: Twelve is the number of non-successional teeth (the molars).
whyNot.1: Sixteen is the number of teeth in one arch.
whyNot.2: Thirty-two is the whole permanent set, including the molars.

explain.body: They let a child chew and speak, support appearance and confidence, and hold space for the permanent teeth. The first permanent molar erupts at about 6 behind them and is often mistaken for a baby tooth.

test.q: A parent thinks their 6-year-old's new back tooth is a baby tooth. Which tooth is it most likely to be?
test.why: The first permanent molar erupts at about 6 years, behind the deciduous second molar, without any baby tooth being lost.

whyNot.0: Deciduous second molars are in place by about 2½ years.
whyNot.2: Second premolars erupt at around 11 to 12 years.
whyNot.3: Canines are at the corner of the arch, not at the back.
